Grind
grīnd
v.t. (rendering Hebrew tachan, Greek alēthō)
From Saxon grindan, to rub or crush small. The daily grinding of grain between two millstones was women's work, done at dawn, and so constant a sound in a town that Scripture uses its silence as a picture of desolation — the sound of the millstones heard no more.

Biblical Definition

Grinding is the humblest daily labour in Scripture, and it becomes the measure of three very different things. It is the work of the humiliated: Samson, blinded and shorn, “did grind in the prison house” (Judges 16:21) — a judge of Israel set to a woman's task at a Philistine mill. It is the instrument of a total destruction, when Moses came down from the mount: he took the calf, “and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Exodus 32:20) — the idol reduced to dust and made to pass through the worshippers. It is the setting of the Lord's warning about the suddenness of His coming: “Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left” (Matthew 24:41) — two women at the same stone, doing the same work, separated for ever in a moment. And it is the prophet's word for what rulers do to the helpless: “What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? saith the Lord GOD of hosts” (Isaiah 3:15). The mill therefore grinds grain, idols, and men — and God notices which.

Webster 1828 Definition

To reduce to powder by friction, as grain between millstones; to oppress. In Scripture, Samson grinding in the prison house, the golden calf ground to powder, two women grinding at the mill when the Son of man comes, and rulers who grind the faces of the poor.

expand to see more

GRIND, v.t. 1. To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction; as, to grind corn between stones.

2. To sharpen by rubbing on a stone; as, to grind an axe.

3. To oppress by severe exactions; to harass; as, to grind the faces of the poor.

4. From Saxon grindan, to grind, to crush small.

5. In Scripture, he did grind in the prison house, Judg. 16; two women shall be grinding at the mill, Matt. 24.

Key Scripture

Judges 16:21 — "But the Philistines took him, and put out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza, and bound him with fetters of brass; and he did grind in the prison house. put"

Exodus 32:20 — "And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it."

Matthew 24:41 — "Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left."

Isaiah 3:15 — "What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? saith the Lord GOD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

Oppression is redefined as an impersonal structural force with no guilty parties, so that the prophets' naming of specific rulers who grind the poor is replaced by a category that convicts nobody.

expand to see more

Isaiah 3:15 is a summons, not a sociological observation. God asks the princes and elders of His people a direct question — what mean ye? — and He names the offence: they have eaten up the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in their houses, and they grind the faces of the poor. Modern discourse handles oppression very differently. It is treated as a structure, an inherited system, or a set of impersonal forces, so that the wrong is universally deplored and nobody in particular is answerable for it. Scripture's method is the opposite: it names Ahab over Naboth's vineyard, David over Uriah, the merchants who make the ephah small and the shekel great. This matters pastorally as well as politically, because a guilt that belongs to a structure cannot be repented of, and a sin that cannot be repented of cannot be forgiven. The prophets left men with somewhere to go.

The opposite failure is to hear those texts as though the Bible had no such concern at all. It has a great deal — the gleaning laws, the jubilee, the prohibition of usury toward a poor brother, the standing warnings to judges who take a bribe, the sharpness of James against rich men who defraud the labourer of his hire. What Scripture will not do is import an oppressor-oppressed grid as the master key to human society; its categories are sin, the fallen heart, and covenant faithfulness, and it convicts poor and rich alike. The principle to recover is exactly Isaiah's: name real wrongs, name the men who do them, require restitution, and preach to both the rich oppressor and the ground-down poor the same gospel of a Redeemer who is no respecter of persons.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tachan, to grind; rechayim, a pair of millstones; daqaq, to crush to powder; Greek alēthō, to grind at a mill, and mylos, a millstone.

expand to see more

Hebrew tachan (H2912) — to grind; the daily labour at the handmill (Numbers 11:8; Judges 16:21).

Hebrew rechayim (H7347) — a pair of millstones; the nether millstone could not be taken in pledge, for it was a man's life (Deuteronomy 24:6).

Hebrew daqaq (H1854) — to crush or beat small; the verb for the golden calf ground to powder (Exodus 32:20).

Greek alēthō (G229) — to grind at a mill; “two women shall be grinding at the mill” (Matthew 24:41).

Greek mylos (G3458) — a millstone; the millstone about the neck of him who offends a little one (Matthew 18:6).

Usage

"Of humiliation and forced labour: he did grind in the prison house (Judges 16:21)."

"Of an idol utterly destroyed: burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder (Exodus 32:20)."

"Of oppression named by God: ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor (Isaiah 3:15)."
